content.content:
1	Temperature-sensitive goods such as vaccines, biological samples, prepared meals and laboratory reagents are frequently shipped in insulated carriers that hold a payload within a target temperature band for a period of hours or days. Carriers of this general kind fall into two broad families. Powered carriers use a fan, a pump or another driven air mover, together with a power source, to force air over a cold source and through the payload space. Passive carriers omit the power source and rely on conduction from, and natural convection around, a refrigerant mass such as water ice, dry ice, gel packs or sealed cassettes charged with a phase-change material.
2	
3	Passive carriers are attractive because they have no battery to charge, no motor to fail and no electrical approval burden for air transport. They are also harder to control. When a refrigerant mass is simply laid on top of, beside or beneath a payload, the cooled air falls where gravity and the packing arrangement happen to send it. Items directly against the refrigerant are driven toward the cold end of the acceptable band or below it, while items on the far side of the payload sit in a stagnant warm layer. The result is a temperature spread across the payload that grows as the load is packed more densely, and that varies from shipment to shipment because it depends on how a particular packer arranged the goods and the refrigerant on a particular day.
4	
5	Attempts to impose a defined circulation path on a passive carrier run into a practical difficulty. The path is defined by clearances, by openings and by the alignment between them, and every one of those relationships is destroyed if the component that carries the openings is set down rotated, offset or skewed by a person working quickly at a packing bench. A carrier that circulates air well when it is assembled precisely, and poorly when it is not, delivers the variability it was intended to remove. Packing instructions, printed arrows and keyed corner blocks all depend on the packer looking, and none of them acts on a component that has already been set down out of position.
6	
7	Two further problems attend repeated reuse of a passive carrier. First, moist ambient air admitted each time the carrier is opened condenses on the cold surfaces of the refrigerant mass and runs down into the payload space, wetting labels and cartons and, over many cycles, leaving standing water in the base of the carrier. Where the refrigerant is a sealed cassette, drying the interior often means removing the cassette from service. Second, a passive carrier gives no account of itself. If the payload was exposed to a temperature excursion in transit, and the refrigerant has since recovered, an inspection at the receiving dock shows a cold carrier and a firm cassette, and the excursion leaves no trace. Electronic data loggers record such events but add cost, battery management and a reading step to every unit shipped, and they report a sensor location rather than the state of the refrigerant that the payload actually depends on.
8	
9	There remains a need for a reusable passive carrier that establishes the same circulation path around the payload every time it is closed, without a powered air mover and without relying on the care of the person who packed it, that manages the condensate produced by repeated opening without taking the refrigerant out of service, and that retains a visible mechanical record of a refrigerant temperature excursion after the refrigerant has recovered.
10

1	In the following description, directional terms such as upper, lower, above, below, inward and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright orientation with the insulated lid uppermost. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.
2	
3	Overall arrangement
4	
5	Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being removable from the outer shell 10.
6	
7	The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12.
8	
9	The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24. The tray side walls 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4.
10	
11	The thermal module
12	
13	Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by a given payload are fitted before packing and exchanged between shipments.
14	
15	The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, located beside the phase-change cassettes, each guide duct 50 lying outboard of an outer face of one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame 42, each peripheral outlet opening 54 being at a lower end of one of the guide ducts 50.
16	
17	The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58 at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame 42. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.
18	
19	Registration and retention by the lid
20	
21	The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 that extends around the underside of the insulated lid 60 outboard of the depending indexing rib 62. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.
22	
23	This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 need only be dropped into the outer shell 10 approximately, and may be set down offset or skewed within the clearance available to it. In the following description, directional terms such as upper, lower, above, below, inward and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright orientation with the insulated lid uppermost. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being removable from the outer shell 10.

The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12.

The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24. The tray side walls 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4.

The thermal module

Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by a given payload are fitted before packing and exchanged between shipments.

The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, located beside the phase-change cassettes, each guide duct 50 lying outboard of an outer face of one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame 42, each peripheral outlet opening 54 being at a lower end of one of the guide ducts 50.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58 at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame 42. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.

Registration and retention by the lid

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 that extends around the underside of the insulated lid 60 outboard of the depending indexing rib 62. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 need only be dropped into the outer shell 10 approximately, and may be set down offset or skewed within the clearance available to it. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is then created by closing the lid, which is an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 project inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10 beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, as seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. The resilient feet 58 maintain a downward holding force during transport, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.

The circulation path

In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the confronting inner faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams that travel outward over the cassette faces. Each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20, from which it rises again through the product region.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Circulation is driven by the density difference between air warmed in the product region and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes. The geometry supports that difference rather than substituting for it: the cooled air is produced at the top of the carrier and is given a continuous downward path of its own along the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, while the warmed air is given a continuous upward path through the product region to the central inlet opening 48, and the two paths meet only at the central inlet opening 48 and beneath the product tray 20. Because the supply and return legs are separated by the tray side walls 26 rather than sharing one opening, the descending cooled stream is not obliged to pass through the ascending warmed stream.

Condensate management

A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough that extends around the product tray 20 at a lower region of the outer shell 10, beneath the side supply passages 28. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70. Discharge openings 76, separate from the peripheral outlet openings 54, are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

Mechanical exposure indicator

The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. Referring to FIG. 6, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44 when the thermal module 40 is in the registered position.

The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.

The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again and the temperature-responsive latch 84 has returned to its retaining condition, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.

Operation

In use, phase-change cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by the payload are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. Goods are placed in the product tray 20 and the product tray 20 is placed in the outer shell 10 so that the tray feet 22 stand on the floor 12, leaving the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20 and the two side supply passages 28 between the tray side walls 26 and the side walls 14. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20. The insulated lid 60 is then closed, whereby the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 and shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position, the resilient feet 58 are pressed against the ledges 18 to retain the thermal module 40, and the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. Air thereafter circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover. At the destination, the insulated lid 60 is opened, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is read and, if it stands in the exposed position, reset manually, the product tray 20 is lifted out with the goods, and the absorbent wick 72 is drawn out by the pull tab 74 and replaced if saturated.

Alternatives

Two phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42, opposed across the central space. Entry of the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 56 during closing travel shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position. The peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74, the discharge openings 76 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features, and a carrier 100 may be built with the registered circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with any combination of the optional features.

The described implementations are examples. A person skilled in the art may combine, substitute or omit the described features within the scope of the claims that follow.

content.text: I've read all inputs, draft sections, numerals, and all six figure briefs. Here is the complete review.

input.summary:
Source ledger traced across draft/01–10, numerals.md and figures/fig-01…06.md against input/disclosure.md and the single USER passage in input/conversation.md (which is verbatim identical to the disclosure). input/brief.md was used only for title, applicant/inventor, no-priority and no-government-support, all of which match draft/01, 02 and 03. The abstract is 141 words and single-paragraph. No drafting notes, placeholders, open questions or unresolved alternatives remain in any file. Numerals.md defines 31 numerals, each used in the description with one meaning, and no numeral appears in a figure brief without a definition.

Most of the skeleton traces cleanly: shell/floor/side walls, tray on feet with lower return passage, tray side walls spaced inward forming two side supply passages, perforations, rigid spacer frame with two opposed cassettes, central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes, peripheral outlet openings aligned with (overlapping) the side supply passages, the full circulation path, absence of fan/pump/powered air mover, depending indexing rib entering a mating channel to shift the module into the registered position, gasket sealing after registration, resilient feet pressed against shell ledges, condensate channel with removable wick and pull tab, guide-duct openings discharging condensate, and the whole exposure-indicator chain (stem thermally coupled to one cassette, temperature-responsive latch, spring, latched exposed position, manual reset after opening, no airflow control). The method claims 18–21 track the disclosure's "For use" paragraph. Background prior-art characterisations are not charged against the inventor sources per instruction.

Fourteen items do not trace, or are internally inconsistent, and are reported below. The most serious is structural: the draft invents a second, distinct set of openings. The disclosure states only "Openings at the lower ends of the guide ducts discharge condensate into the channel," yet the draft places peripheral outlet openings 54 at the lower ends of the guide ducts and then asserts discharge openings 76 that are "separate from the peripheral outlet openings 54" — in the Summary, the description, dependent claims 8 and 17, and FIG. 5. Nothing in the sources affirms two separate sets; that separateness is a new limitation and is reported critical.

Three further disclosure-fidelity gaps are reported major: (a) the convection mechanism and flow-topology reasoning added at Summary ¶5 and description ¶31 ("Circulation is driven by the density difference…", "the two paths meet only at the central inlet opening 48 and beneath the product tray 20", "the descending cooled stream is not obliged to pass through the ascending warmed stream"), for which the only source wording is "Warm air rising from the product region enters the central inlet"; (b) the inner-face/outer-face crossover topology ("two cooling streams that travel outward over the cassette faces", "each guide duct 50 lying outboard of an outer face", claim 5, and FIG. 2's cassette upper edges drawn below the frame top edges so air crosses over the cassettes), where the source says only "divides along faces of the cassettes" and "two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes"; and (c) the dependent-claim 7 positional limitation "at a lower region of the outer shell beneath the side supply passages", where the source says only "a shallow condensate channel around the product tray".

Four verified internal inconsistencies are reported major. First, the mating channel 56 is placed in FIG. 2 on "the top edge of the left short end wall" but FIG. 3 — an enlargement of an upper side region of FIG. 1, in the same fragment as ledge 18 and resilient foot 58, which FIG. 2 puts on the long side — shows the groove there; one section plane cannot contain both. Second, FIG. 1's Geometry-to-draw omits every feature its own enlargements are said to enlarge: no indexing rib 62, gasket 64, ledge 18, perforations 30, condensate channel 70 or wick 72 appear in the parent view, so FIG. 3, FIG. 4 and FIG. 5 enlarge regions that do not contain the detail. Third, FIG. 6 draws the coil spring 86 "shown compressed" while the stem stands in the exposed position, contradicting description ¶41 and claim 10, in which the spring biases the stem toward the exposed position and moves it there on release. Fourth, FIG. 4 draws perforations 30 passing through the tray side wall "from its left surface to its right surface", i.e. into the tray interior, while description ¶9 says they "open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24"; FIG. 4 shows no tray bottom wall, so as briefed the flow path contradicts both the description and the disclosed order "enters the side supply passages, passes through perforations in the product tray, and returns through the lower return passage".

Six minor items are reported: the gasket's unsourced "extends around an underside … outboard of the depending indexing rib" (claim 4, ¶21); the unsourced siting of ledges as inward projections of the side walls and feet at "lower outboard regions" (claims 2, 15, 16, ¶17, ¶25); two unsourced indicator qualifiers ("when the thermal module 40 is in the registered position"; "the temperature-responsive latch 84 has returned to its retaining condition") together with FIG. 6 drawing the stem's inner end spaced across a gap from cassette 44 despite the recited thermal coupling; the Brief Description's narrowing of the perforations to "a tray side wall" against the description's "through the product tray 20"; the unsourced skew-correction capability ("offset or skewed", Summary ¶7 and ¶23); and two FIG. 2 briefing defects — numeral 40 targeted onto the spacer frame's own wall where it cannot be distinguished from 42, and an unsourced count of "a horizontal row of rectangular openings" per guide duct.

Section-line check: no view uses a named section-line designation, so there is no cross-view designation mismatch; FIG. 1 and FIG. 6 are self-standing sectional views and FIGS. 3–5 are enlargements, all designated consistently in 07-drawings.md and in the figure briefs. No section-line finding is raised on that basis; the FIG. 1/enlargement content mismatch is reported separately above.

Per input/brief.md, no prior-art search was run, and the art present in prior_art/ may be incomplete; Background characterisations are left for the later citation review.

findings.title: Discharge openings recited as "separate from the peripheral outlet openings" are not disclosed as a separate set
findings.where: draft/06-summary.md ¶9; draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶35; draft/09-claims.md claims 8 and 17; figures/fig-05.md (numeral 76)
findings.detail: The draft first places the peripheral outlet openings 54 "at lower ends of the guide ducts" (claim 1, claim 14, description ¶15) and then recites a second, distinct set of openings at the same location, expressly "separate from the peripheral outlet openings". The disclosure describes only one set of openings at the lower ends of the guide ducts, and does not say the condensate openings are distinct from the air-outlet openings. The separateness is an added structural limitation appearing in two independent-claim-dependent claims and in the figure briefs, and no affirmative source passage supports it. The nearest source passage shows the gap: it names the openings only by their location and function, with no distinction drawn.
findings.evidence: Candidate (claim 8): "wherein the guide ducts have discharge openings, separate from the peripheral outlet openings, at lower ends of the guide ducts". Candidate (claim 17): "discharge openings, separate from the peripheral outlet openings, at the lower ends of the guide ducts". Candidate (¶35): "Discharge openings 76, separate from the peripheral outlet openings 54, are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50". Nearest source (disclosure ¶11 / conversation USER ¶13): "Openings at the lower ends of the guide ducts discharge condensate into the channel." No source passage states that these openings are separate from, or additional to, the peripheral outlet openings.
findings.fix: Delete the separateness limitation everywhere. In claim 8 read: "wherein openings at lower ends of the guide ducts discharge condensate into the condensate channel." In claim 17 read: "wherein openings at the lower ends of the guide ducts are positioned to discharge condensate into a condensate channel of the outer shell." In ¶35 read: "Discharge openings 76 at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70." In Summary ¶9 delete ", separate from the peripheral outlet openings,". In figures/fig-05.md keep numeral 76 on the opening at the lower end of the guide duct without implying a second set.

findings.title: Convection driving mechanism and flow-separation reasoning have no affirmative source passage
findings.detail: The draft asserts a physical driving mechanism (buoyancy from a density difference) and a topological exclusivity (the two streams meet only at two named places, and the descending stream need not pass through the ascending stream). The disclosure states only that the carrier is passive, that it has no fan, pump or powered air mover, and that warm air rises from the product region into the central inlet. It says nothing about density difference, about where the two streams do or do not meet, or about the supply and return legs being separated by the tray side walls. These are asserted results and relationships, not mere restatement of the disclosed path.
findings.evidence: Candidate (¶31): "Circulation is driven by the density difference between air warmed in the product region and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes. The geometry supports that difference rather than substituting for it: ... and the two paths meet only at the central inlet opening 48 and beneath the product tray 20. Because the supply and return legs are separated by the tray side walls 26 rather than sharing one opening, the descending cooled stream is not obliged to pass through the ascending warmed stream." Candidate (Summary ¶5): "and the circulation is driven by the density difference between the air warmed in the product region and the air cooled along the cassette faces." Nearest source (disclosure ¶7): "Warm air rising from the product region enters the central inlet, divides along faces of the cassettes, descends through the guide ducts ... The carrier is passive. It has no fan, pump, or powered air mover."
findings.fix: In ¶31 replace the quoted sentences with: "The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Air warmed in the product region rises to the central inlet opening 48, and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes descends through the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, so that circulation proceeds without any powered air mover." In Summary ¶5 delete ", and the circulation is driven by the density difference between the air warmed in the product region and the air cooled along the cassette faces".

findings.title: Inner-face/outer-face duct topology and the over-the-cassette crossover are not in the sources
findings.where: draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶13, ¶15, ¶29; draft/09-claims.md claim 5; figures/fig-02.md ("its upper edge below the top edges of the frame walls")
findings.detail: The disclosure says the ducts are "beside the cassettes" and that air "divides along faces of the cassettes". The draft converts this into a specific topology: the stream divides along the confronting inner faces, travels outward over the cassette faces, and then descends in ducts lying outboard of the outer faces; FIG. 2 additionally briefs the cassette upper edges as standing below the frame top edges, which is the structure that would let air cross over each cassette from the central space to the outboard channel. The crossover path, the assignment of the dividing flow to the inner faces, and the ducts' position outboard of the outer faces are technical substance with no affirmative source passage, and the ducts' position is recited as a dependent-claim limitation.
findings.evidence: Candidate (¶15): "each guide duct 50 lying outboard of an outer face of one of the phase-change cassettes". Candidate (¶29): "The rising stream divides along the confronting inner faces ... giving two cooling streams that travel outward over the cassette faces." Candidate (claim 5): "and each guide duct lies outboard of an outer face of one of the phase-change cassettes." Candidate (fig-02.md): "Each slab is a plain closed box, shown schematically, its upper edge below the top edges of the frame walls." Nearest source (disclosure ¶7): "It includes a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes ... Warm air rising from the product region enters the central inlet, divides along faces of the cassettes, descends through the guide ducts".
findings.fix: In ¶15 read "each guide duct 50 lying beside one of the phase-change cassettes". In ¶29 read "The rising stream divides along the faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams, and each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes". Delete the final clause of claim 5 ("and each guide duct lies outboard of an outer face of one of the phase-change cassettes"). In figures/fig-02.md replace the quoted sentence with: "Each slab is a plain closed box, shown schematically."

findings.title: Mating channel 56 is located on the short end wall in FIG. 2 but on the enlarged side region in FIG. 1/FIG. 3
findings.where: figures/fig-02.md ("top edge of the left short end wall"); figures/fig-03.md; draft/07-drawings.md FIG. 3
findings.detail: FIG. 3 is briefed as an enlargement of an upper side region of FIG. 1 and contains, in one fragment, the ledge 18 projecting from a side wall 14, the resilient foot 58 on that ledge, and the mating channel 56 in the upper edge of the spacer frame. FIG. 2 places the resilient feet on the long side ("two visible at the front") and the peripheral outlet openings in the long side walls, but places the mating channel on the top edge of the left short end wall. A single vertical section taken across the long side walls, as FIG. 1 is briefed (two upright blocks with a channel outboard of each opening through the outboard side), cannot contain a groove located in the short end wall. The same designated part 56 is therefore shown in two mutually exclusive positions.
findings.evidence: figures/fig-02.md: "The top edge of the left short end wall carries an upwardly open groove running across the full depth of that wall from front to back. This groove is the mating channel 56." figures/fig-03.md: "Its upper edge carries an upwardly open groove whose width matches the thickness of the depending indexing rib 62 ... This groove is the mating channel 56" — in the same fragment as "one of the ledges 18" projecting from "one of the side walls 14" and "one of the resilient feet 58". draft/07-drawings.md: "FIG. 3 is an enlarged view of an upper side region of FIG. 1, showing the depending indexing rib engaged in the mating channel, ... and a resilient foot of the spacer frame pressed against a ledge of a side wall of the outer shell."
findings.fix: In figures/fig-02.md relocate the groove to the wall shown enlarged in FIG. 3: replace the quoted sentence with "The top edge of the near long side wall carries an upwardly open groove at mid-length, running across the thickness of that wall. This groove is the mating channel 56.", and move numeral target 56 to "well inside the groove in the top edge of the near long side wall".

findings.title: FIG. 1 omits every feature that FIGS. 3, 4 and 5 are briefed to enlarge
findings.where: figures/fig-01.md "Geometry to draw"; draft/07-drawings.md FIG. 3, FIG. 4, FIG. 5
findings.detail: FIGS. 3, 4 and 5 are each designated an enlarged view of a named region of FIG. 1, yet FIG. 1's geometry contains none of the parts those enlargements show: no depending indexing rib on the lid underside, no lid gasket at the shell upper edge, no ledges on the side walls, no perforations in the tray walls, no condensate channel in the floor and no wick. FIG. 1 briefs the tray walls as continuous and the floor top surface as plain and flat where the feet stand, which is affirmatively inconsistent with a perforated tray side wall (FIG. 4) and with a trough sunk in the floor top surface at the foot of the side gap (FIG. 5). An enlarged view must enlarge a region that exists in the parent view.
findings.evidence: figures/fig-01.md: "a horizontal slab lies across the top ends of both wall bodies ... This slab is the insulated lid 60, closed. That interface is shown enlarged in FIG. 3" (no rib, no gasket, no ledge briefed anywhere in the file); "its outer side surfaces stand clear of the inner surfaces of the wall bodies, leaving an open vertical gap on each side running from the top of the box down to the floor 12" (no perforations, no trough). Compare figures/fig-03.md (rib 62, gasket 64, ledge 18), figures/fig-04.md ("These openings are the perforations 30") and figures/fig-05.md ("This trough is the condensate channel 70").
findings.fix: Add to figures/fig-01.md, in Geometry to draw: "A narrow rib projects downward from the underside of the slab on each side, inboard of the top ends of the wall bodies, and a small compressible body lies between the slab underside and each top end. A block projects inward from the inner surface of each wall body just below the elongated upper body. A series of small openings passes through the lower portion of each upright wall of the open-top box, below the level of its bottom wall. A shallow upwardly open trough is formed in the top surface of the floor 12 at the foot of each vertical gap, with an elongated absorbent body lying in it." Leave these unnumbered on FIG. 1; they are numbered in FIGS. 3, 4 and 5.

findings.title: FIG. 6 shows the spring compressed while the stem stands in the exposed position it is biased toward
findings.detail: The description and claim 10 recite a spring biasing the indicator stem toward the exposed position, which the spring drives the stem into when the latch releases. FIG. 6 is briefed with the stem in the exposed position and the spring "shown compressed", which depicts the spring as still storing the energy it is said to have already released. The figure therefore contradicts the recited operation of the same numbered parts 82 and 86.
findings.evidence: figures/fig-06.md View: "seen horizontally with the indicator stem in the exposed position"; Geometry: "A coil spring surrounds the shaft within the outline, drawn as aligned loops and shown compressed. This spring is the spring 86." draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶41: "a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position"; ¶43: "On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position".
findings.fix: In figures/fig-06.md replace "drawn as aligned loops and shown compressed" with "drawn as aligned loops and shown extended, its loops spaced apart".

findings.title: FIG. 4 draws the perforations opening into the tray interior, not into the lower return passage
findings.where: figures/fig-04.md ("from its left surface to its right surface"); draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶9
findings.detail: The description states that the perforations open from the side supply passages into the lower return passage, which matches the disclosed flow order. FIG. 4 shows no tray bottom wall and no lower return passage, and briefs the perforations as passing through the tray side wall from its left surface (the side supply passage) to its right surface, which in the fragment as briefed is the interior of the tray. As drawn, the descending stream would enter the product region directly instead of returning beneath the tray, contradicting both the description and the disclosed path.
findings.evidence: figures/fig-04.md: "In the lower portion of the thin wall, a series of small openings passes through it from its left surface to its right surface, shown schematically. These openings are the perforations 30." draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶9: "Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24." Source (disclosure ¶7): "enters the side supply passages, passes through perforations in the product tray, and returns through the lower return passage."
findings.fix: In figures/fig-04.md add, before the perforations sentence: "A thin hatched horizontal bottom wall joins the thin upright wall and extends rightward, and the open space beneath that bottom wall is the lower return passage 24." Then read: "In the portion of the thin upright wall below that bottom wall, a series of small openings passes through it, so that the side supply passage 28 opens through them into the space beneath the bottom wall. These openings are the perforations 30." Add 24 to the sheet numeral list with target "inside the open space beneath the thin horizontal bottom wall".

findings.title: Condensate channel located "at a lower region of the outer shell beneath the side supply passages" without source
findings.detail: The disclosure locates the condensate channel only by reference to the product tray. The draft adds a positional limitation placing it at a lower region of the outer shell and vertically beneath the side supply passages, and recites that position in dependent claim 7. No affirmative source passage places the channel below the side supply passages or in the shell rather than around the tray.
findings.evidence: Candidate (claim 7): "a condensate channel extending around the product tray at a lower region of the outer shell beneath the side supply passages". Candidate (¶35): "A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough that extends around the product tray 20 at a lower region of the outer shell 10, beneath the side supply passages 28." Nearest source (disclosure ¶11): "A removable absorbent wick lies in a shallow condensate channel around the product tray."
findings.fix: In claim 7 read: "further comprising a shallow condensate channel extending around the product tray, and a removable absorbent wick lying in the condensate channel." In ¶35 read: "A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough that extends around the product tray 20."

findings.title: Gasket geometry "extends around an underside ... outboard of the depending indexing rib" is unsourced
findings.detail: The disclosure states only that a compressible lid gasket seals against the upper edge of the shell after registration. The draft adds that the gasket runs continuously around the lid underside and that it is outboard of the indexing rib, and recites that geometry as dependent claim 4.
findings.evidence: Candidate (claim 4): "wherein the compressible lid gasket extends around an underside of the insulated lid outboard of the depending indexing rib." Candidate (¶21): "a compressible lid gasket 64 that extends around the underside of the insulated lid 60 outboard of the depending indexing rib 62". Nearest source (disclosure ¶9): "A compressible lid gasket seals against the upper edge of the shell after registration."
findings.fix: Cancel claim 4 and renumber claims 5–13 as 4–12, with the dependencies of the renumbered claims adjusted accordingly. In ¶21 read: "and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10."

findings.title: Ledges sited on the side walls and feet sited at "lower outboard regions" without source
findings.detail: The disclosure refers to "ledges of the shell" and "resilient feet of the spacer frame" without locating either. The draft fixes the ledges as inward projections of the side walls and the feet (and the peripheral outlet openings) at lower outboard regions of the frame, and recites those locations in claims 2, 15 and 16.
findings.evidence: Candidate (¶25): "Ledges 18 project inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10 beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42". Candidate (claim 2): "the side walls of the outer shell have ledges beneath the resilient feet". Candidate (claim 16): "the peripheral outlet openings are located at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame." Nearest source (disclosure ¶9): "The same closing movement presses resilient feet of the spacer frame against ledges of the shell so that the module cannot lift away from the tray during transport."
findings.fix: In claim 2 read: "wherein the spacer frame carries resilient feet, the outer shell has ledges beneath the resilient feet, and closure of the insulated lid presses the resilient feet against the ledges so that the thermal module is held down against lifting away from the product tray." In claim 15 read "resilient feet carried by the spacer frame" in place of "resilient feet at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame". In claim 16 delete ", and the peripheral outlet openings are located at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame". In ¶25 read: "Ledges 18 of the outer shell 10 lie beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42".

findings.title: Indicator qualifiers and FIG. 6's gap between stem and cassette are unsourced

findings.evidence: Candidate (¶41): "The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44 when the thermal module 40 is in the registered position." Candidate (¶45): "after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again and the temperature-responsive latch 84 has returned to its retaining condition". Candidate (fig-06.md): "its left face confronting the inner end of the shaft across the intervening space." Nearest source (disclosure ¶13): "An indicator stem is thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette and retained by a temperature-responsive latch. ... The indication remains exposed after the cassette cools again".
findings.fix: In ¶41 read: "The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44." In ¶45 delete "and the temperature-responsive latch 84 has returned to its retaining condition". In figures/fig-06.md read: "its left face contacting the inner end of the shaft, so that the two are in thermal contact."

findings.title: Brief Description narrows the perforations to a tray side wall
findings.detail: The claims and the description locate the perforations generically "through the product tray 20", matching the source. The Brief Description of FIG. 4 assigns them to a tray side wall, introducing a placement the sources do not state and using a designation that differs from the description and claims for the same numbered part 30.
findings.evidence: Candidate (07-drawings.md): "FIG. 4 is an enlarged view of a lower side region of FIG. 1, showing a peripheral outlet opening at the foot of a guide duct, a side supply passage, and perforations of a tray side wall." findings.title: FIG. 2 numeral 40 cannot be distinguished from 42, and the outlet-opening count is unsourced

Source ledger traced across draft/01–10, numerals.md and figures/fig-01…06.md against input/disclosure.md and the single USER passage in input/conversation.md (which is verbatim identical to the disclosure). input/brief.md was used only for title, applicant/inventor, no-priority and no-government-support, all of which match draft/01, 02 and 03. The abstract is 141 words and single-paragraph. No drafting notes, placeholders, open questions or unresolved alternatives remain in any file. Numerals.md defines 31 numerals, each used in the description with one meaning, and no numeral appears in a figure brief without a definition.

Most of the skeleton traces cleanly: shell/floor/side walls, tray on feet with lower return passage, tray side walls spaced inward forming two side supply passages, perforations, rigid spacer frame with two opposed cassettes, central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes, peripheral outlet openings aligned with (overlapping) the side supply passages, the full circulation path, absence of fan/pump/powered air mover, depending indexing rib entering a mating channel to shift the module into the registered position, gasket sealing after registration, resilient feet pressed against shell ledges, condensate channel with removable wick and pull tab, guide-duct openings discharging condensate, and the whole exposure-indicator chain (stem thermally coupled to one cassette, temperature-responsive latch, spring, latched exposed position, manual reset after opening, no airflow control). The method claims 18–21 track the disclosure's "For use" paragraph. Background prior-art characterisations are not charged against the inventor sources per instruction.

Fourteen items do not trace, or are internally inconsistent, and are reported below. The most serious is structural: the draft invents a second, distinct set of openings. The disclosure states only "Openings at the lower ends of the guide ducts discharge condensate into the channel," yet the draft places peripheral outlet openings 54 at the lower ends of the guide ducts and then asserts discharge openings 76 that are "separate from the peripheral outlet openings 54" — in the Summary, the description, dependent claims 8 and 17, and FIG. 5. Nothing in the sources affirms two separate sets; that separateness is a new limitation and is reported critical.

Three further disclosure-fidelity gaps are reported major: (a) the convection mechanism and flow-topology reasoning added at Summary ¶5 and description ¶31 ("Circulation is driven by the density difference…", "the two paths meet only at the central inlet opening 48 and beneath the product tray 20", "the descending cooled stream is not obliged to pass through the ascending warmed stream"), for which the only source wording is "Warm air rising from the product region enters the central inlet"; (b) the inner-face/outer-face crossover topology ("two cooling streams that travel outward over the cassette faces", "each guide duct 50 lying outboard of an outer face", claim 5, and FIG. 2's cassette upper edges drawn below the frame top edges so air crosses over the cassettes), where the source says only "divides along faces of the cassettes" and "two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes"; and (c) the dependent-claim 7 positional limitation "at a lower region of the outer shell beneath the side supply passages", where the source says only "a shallow condensate channel around the product tray".

Four verified internal inconsistencies are reported major. First, the mating channel 56 is placed in FIG. 2 on "the top edge of the left short end wall" but FIG. 3 — an enlargement of an upper side region of FIG. 1, in the same fragment as ledge 18 and resilient foot 58, which FIG. 2 puts on the long side — shows the groove there; one section plane cannot contain both. Second, FIG. 1's Geometry-to-draw omits every feature its own enlargements are said to enlarge: no indexing rib 62, gasket 64, ledge 18, perforations 30, condensate channel 70 or wick 72 appear in the parent view, so FIG. 3, FIG. 4 and FIG. 5 enlarge regions that do not contain the detail. Third, FIG. 6 draws the coil spring 86 "shown compressed" while the stem stands in the exposed position, contradicting description ¶41 and claim 10, in which the spring biases the stem toward the exposed position and moves it there on release. Fourth, FIG. 4 draws perforations 30 passing through the tray side wall "from its left surface to its right surface", i.e. into the tray interior, while description ¶9 says they "open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24"; FIG. 4 shows no tray bottom wall, so as briefed the flow path contradicts both the description and the disclosed order "enters the side supply passages, passes through perforations in the product tray, and returns through the lower return passage".

Six minor items are reported: the gasket's unsourced "extends around an underside … outboard of the depending indexing rib" (claim 4, ¶21); the unsourced siting of ledges as inward projections of the side walls and feet at "lower outboard regions" (claims 2, 15, 16, ¶17, ¶25); two unsourced indicator qualifiers ("when the thermal module 40 is in the registered position"; "the temperature-responsive latch 84 has returned to its retaining condition") together with FIG. 6 drawing the stem's inner end spaced across a gap from cassette 44 despite the recited thermal coupling; the Brief Description's narrowing of the perforations to "a tray side wall" against the description's "through the product tray 20"; the unsourced skew-correction capability ("offset or skewed", Summary ¶7 and ¶23); and two FIG. 2 briefing defects — numeral 40 targeted onto the spacer frame's own wall where it cannot be distinguished from 42, and an unsourced count of "a horizontal row of rectangular openings" per guide duct.

Section-line check: no view uses a named section-line designation, so there is no cross-view designation mismatch; FIG. 1 and FIG. 6 are self-standing sectional views and FIGS. 3–5 are enlargements, all designated consistently in 07-drawings.md and in the figure briefs. No section-line finding is raised on that basis; the FIG. 1/enlargement content mismatch is reported separately above.

Per input/brief.md, no prior-art search was run, and the art present in prior_art/ may be incomplete; Background characterisations are left for the later citation review.

findings.title: Convection driving mechanism and flow-separation reasoning have no affirmative source passage
findings.detail: The draft asserts a physical driving mechanism (buoyancy from a density difference) and a topological exclusivity (the two streams meet only at two named places, and the descending stream need not pass through the ascending stream). The disclosure states only that the carrier is passive, that it has no fan, pump or powered air mover, and that warm air rises from the product region into the central inlet. It says nothing about density difference, about where the two streams do or do not meet, or about the supply and return legs being separated by the tray side walls. These are asserted results and relationships, not mere restatement of the disclosed path.
findings.evidence: Candidate (¶31): "Circulation is driven by the density difference between air warmed in the product region and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes. The geometry supports that difference rather than substituting for it: ... and the two paths meet only at the central inlet opening 48 and beneath the product tray 20. Because the supply and return legs are separated by the tray side walls 26 rather than sharing one opening, the descending cooled stream is not obliged to pass through the ascending warmed stream." Candidate (Summary ¶5): "and the circulation is driven by the density difference between the air warmed in the product region and the air cooled along the cassette faces." Nearest source (disclosure ¶7): "Warm air rising from the product region enters the central inlet, divides along faces of the cassettes, descends through the guide ducts ... The carrier is passive. It has no fan, pump, or powered air mover."

Air warmed in the product region rises to the central inlet opening 48, and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes descends through the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, so that circulation proceeds without any powered air mover." In Summary ¶5 delete ", and the circulation is driven by the density difference between the air warmed in the product region and the air cooled along the cassette faces".
